narrative:
The model predicted a 62.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking after the first year of law school and your class ranking after the third year were the two strongest influences, both pushing the prediction toward failure. Compared with students who were accepted, you placed much lower in your class in both periods—second decile versus an average around sixth decile for accepted applicants. These consistently lower standings signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, and it worked in the opposite direction. At 36, your score is only slightly below the 37.2 average of accepted students, so it provided a modest pull toward passing. However, it was not strong enough to overcome the negative effect of your class rankings.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0 (versus 3.23 average), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time had smaller effects and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most influenced this decision. (218 words)
